title: HOW OLD WAS ESAU WHEN HE MARRIED HIS FIRST TWO WIVES? THE ANSWER IS 40—BUT THE HEARTBREAK BEHIND GENESIS 26:34 IS SOMETHING EVERY FAMILY NEEDS TO HEAR
paragraphs: HOW OLD WAS ESAU WHEN HE MARRIED HIS FIRST TWO WIVES? THE ANSWER IS 40—BUT THE HEARTBREAK BEHIND GENESIS 26:34 IS SOMETHING EVERY FAMILY NEEDS TO HEAR

He was old enough to marry, old enough to make his own decisions, and old enough to know his family's spiritual heritage. But one decision would bring bitterness into the home of Isaac and Rebekah. Behind this overlooked verse is a devastating warning about choices, spiritual compromise, parental heartbreak, and the grace of God that can reach even the most complicated family.
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't come from losing someone to death.
It comes from watching someone you love make decisions that slowly carry them away from everything you prayed they would become.
A father watches his son grow into a man, yet wonders whether the faith he tried to pass down ever truly reached his heart.
A mother remembers holding her child when he was helpless, teaching him what was right, praying over his future, and believing that one day he would walk faithfully with God.
Then the child grows up.
He begins making his own decisions.
And suddenly, the parents discover something painful.
You can raise a child in a home that knows God without being able to guarantee that the child will choose God's ways.
That is part of the sorrow waiting inside Genesis 26:34–35.
And what makes this passage so unsettling is that the Bible does not begin with a dramatic scandal, a violent confrontation, or a public catastrophe.
It begins with a man's age.
Forty.
Just one number.

But behind that number is a family story involving spiritual inheritance, parental grief, divided loyalties, wounded relationships, and choices whose consequences would reach far beyond one household.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
Before we finish looking at Esau, we may discover something about ourselves.
Scripture says:
"And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah."
— Genesis 26:34–35, KJV
There is the direct biblical answer.
Esau was forty years old when he married Judith and Bashemath, his first two wives named in Genesis 26:34.
The text identifies Judith as the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Bashemath as the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
It does not provide two separate wedding dates. It presents both marriages in connection with Esau being forty years old.
That is what Scripture tells us.
But if we stop at the number, we miss the human anguish that the next verse reveals.
Because the real emotional weight of the passage is not simply that Esau married.
It is what those marriages meant within the story of a family entrusted with God's covenant promises.
And to understand that, we need to return to something that happened long before Esau turned forty.
Before there were wives, before there was parental grief, before the family became divided by deception and resentment, there were two brothers struggling inside their mother's womb.
Rebekah was pregnant with twins.
The struggle was so troubling that she sought the LORD.
God answered her:
"Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger."
— Genesis 25:23, KJV
Even before Esau and Jacob were born, God had revealed that their family history would unfold in an extraordinary way.
These were not merely two boys who would grow up with different personalities.
They would become ancestors of peoples whose histories would be intertwined.
Esau would become associated with Edom.
Jacob would receive the name Israel.
But being born into a family connected to God's covenant did not automatically produce a heart that treasured the things of God.
And this is where Esau's story begins to disturb us.
Genesis 25 describes Esau as a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quieter man who dwelt in tents.
Their father Isaac loved Esau, particularly because he enjoyed the game Esau brought home. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Already, we see a household vulnerable to favoritism.
Already, there are fractures.
And then comes the incident involving the birthright.
Esau returns from the field exhausted and hungry.
Jacob has prepared food.
Esau wants something to eat.
Jacob demands his birthright in exchange.
And Esau agrees.
Genesis 25:34 ends with a devastating statement:
"Thus Esau despised his birthright."
The Hebrew expression is:
וַיִּבֶז עֵשָׂו אֶת־הַבְּכֹרָה
Vayyivez Esav et-habekhorah.
Meaning, in context:
"So Esau despised the birthright."
The verb translated "despised" comes from the Hebrew root בָּזָה (bazah), which conveys treating something as insignificant, holding it in contempt, or failing to give it its proper value.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Esau had no appetite.
He was hungry.
It does not say his physical need was imaginary.
His exhaustion was real.
The problem was that he treated something of lasting importance as though it were worth surrendering for immediate satisfaction.
And that is a warning that reaches across centuries.
Sometimes the most dangerous decisions are not made when we hate what is holy.
Sometimes they are made when we want something else more urgently.
We know what matters.
We know what we have been taught.
We know what God has said.
But something in front of us begins to feel more important than everything we might lose.
One moment of anger.
One secret relationship.
One dishonest transaction.
One temptation we have been entertaining for too long.
One decision we tell ourselves we can undo later.
And suddenly, we discover that a temporary appetite can produce consequences that last far longer than the satisfaction it promised.
That does not mean every mistake is irreversible.
The Gospel is full of hope for repentant sinners.
But grace does not make wisdom unnecessary.
And forgiveness does not mean our decisions have no earthly consequences.
Now return to Esau at forty.
There is an important detail here that is easy to overlook.
Genesis 25:26 tells us Isaac was sixty years old when Rebekah gave birth to Esau and Jacob.
Therefore, when Esau was forty, Isaac was approximately one hundred years old.
This was not a family without history.
Isaac had lived through decades of God's provision.
He was the son of Abraham, the child whose birth had testified to God's faithfulness to His promise.
And Isaac himself had married Rebekah when he was forty years old, according to Genesis 25:20.
Do you see the striking parallel?
Isaac was forty when he married Rebekah. Esau was forty when he married Judith and Bashemath.
The same age.
But very different marriage narratives.
In Genesis 24, Abraham had been deeply concerned that Isaac should not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he lived.
He sent his servant to seek a wife from his own kin.
That concern belonged to the specific covenant history of Abraham's family. It was not a declaration that one ethnicity was inherently superior to another.
The issue was preserving covenant faithfulness in a world filled with competing religious loyalties.
The servant prayed.
God providentially guided the journey.
Rebekah entered the story.
And the account culminated in a marriage that continued the covenant family line.
Then, one generation later, Genesis tells us that Esau married two Hittite women.
And the immediate result recorded in Scripture is grief.
The Hebrew of Genesis 26:35 reads:
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה
Vattihyeyna morat ruach le-Yitzchaq ule-Rivqah.
The expression מֹרַת רוּחַ (morat ruach) communicates bitterness or distress of spirit.
A close English rendering is:
"And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah."
The KJV says "a grief of mind."
The Hebrew wording helps us feel the depth of the statement.
This was not presented as a minor family disagreement.
It was deep distress.
Something about these marriages brought real bitterness into the lives of Isaac and Rebekah.
We must be careful here.
Genesis 26:35 does not give us a detailed record of Judith's or Bashemath's personal conduct. It does not quote their conversations or tell us every reason for the parents' distress.
We should not invent accusations against these women that Scripture itself does not make.

What the broader narrative does show is a longstanding concern about marriage alliances with the Canaanite peoples, a concern later made explicit by Isaac when he instructed Jacob not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan (Genesis 28:1).
Genesis 27:46 also records Rebekah's anguish concerning the Hittite women.
So the passage belongs to a larger biblical concern about covenant identity, household loyalty, and the preservation of faith.
The spiritual danger was not someone's ancestry by itself.
Throughout Scripture, God welcomes people from outside Israel who turn to Him in faith.
Rahab was welcomed.
Ruth the Moabite became part of the ancestry of David and, ultimately, the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ.
The issue is never that God's mercy belongs to only one ethnic group.
The issue is whether people will honor the true God or turn their hearts toward idols.
And that brings us to a question that every believer should consider.
Are we making decisions that honor God, or are we expecting God to bless decisions we have already made without seeking Him?
Because there is a difference.
We can pray for God's blessing while refusing to submit our desires to His Word.
We can ask God to protect our relationships while ignoring the spiritual direction in which those relationships are carrying us.
We can speak about faith publicly while making our most important decisions as though God's wisdom has nothing to say.
And sometimes the people who see the danger first are those who love us most.
But there is another side to this story.
Perhaps you are not identifying with Esau.
Perhaps you are identifying with Isaac and Rebekah.
You know what it is to pray for someone who keeps choosing a painful path.
You have tried to speak gently.
You have tried to warn them.
You have watched them dismiss advice that came from love.
And there are nights when you wonder whether anything you taught them still matters.
There is a special kind of helplessness in loving someone whose choices you cannot control.
You cannot repent on their behalf.
You cannot manufacture faith inside their heart.
You cannot force spiritual maturity through fear, arguments, or endless reminders.
You can speak truth.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can set appropriate boundaries.
But you cannot become the Holy Spirit in someone else's life.
And if that describes your pain, remember this:
Your inability to control another person's choices does not mean God has lost the ability to reach that person.
The story of Esau, however, also warns parents against imagining that every family wound belongs entirely to the children.
Isaac and Rebekah were not flawless.
Their favoritism toward different sons helped create a deeply divided household.
Later, Jacob would deceive his father, Rebekah would participate in the scheme, and Esau would become furious over the blessing he lost.
Genesis does not present this family as a collection of perfect saints surrounded by one troublesome son.
It presents human beings.
Complicated human beings.
People who had received extraordinary promises from God but still struggled with fear, favoritism, manipulation, appetite, and resentment.
And isn't that what makes the Bible so painfully believable?
It does not pretend that families connected to God's purposes are automatically free from dysfunction.
It does not conceal the failures of patriarchs.
It does not erase the tears.
It does not sanitize the consequences.
It tells the truth.
And then it shows us that God remains faithful even when human beings are not.
That does not mean God approves of deception, compromise, or family cruelty.
It means His redemptive purposes are not dependent upon human perfection.
There is also an important complication in the later genealogical records.
Genesis 28:9 reports that Esau subsequently married Mahalath, a daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth.
Genesis 36:2–3 gives another account of Esau's wives, naming Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah daughter of Anah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth.
These lists do not match the names and family descriptions in Genesis 26:34 in a simple one-to-one way.
Some interpreters have suggested that certain women had multiple names. Others understand the lists differently. Scripture does not explicitly explain every difference.
It would therefore be careless to pretend that all the naming questions are conclusively settled.
But the uncertainty concerning the later lists does not erase the clear statement in Genesis 26:34.
Esau was forty when he took Judith and Bashemath as wives, according to that verse.
And Genesis immediately tells us that these marriages brought grief to his parents.
Now consider what happens next in the larger narrative.
In Genesis 28:8–9, Esau recognizes that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to his father Isaac.
He then takes another wife from Ishmael's family.
It is a revealing moment.
Esau appears to be responding to his father's displeasure.
But the text does not tell us that this action amounted to spiritual repentance or a complete change of heart.
And that distinction matters.
Because changing an outward decision is not necessarily the same as surrendering the inward person to God.
Someone can change relationships to gain approval.
Someone can begin attending church because of family pressure.
Someone can adopt religious language to repair a reputation.
Those outward actions may be meaningful.
But true repentance goes deeper than appearance.
It is not merely asking, "How do I make people stop being disappointed in me?"
It is asking, "Lord, where have I sinned against You, and how must my heart change?"
The New Testament gives us another sobering perspective on Esau.
Hebrews 12:16–17 warns believers against becoming sexually immoral or profane, using Esau as an example of someone who sold his birthright for a single meal.
The Greek word used to describe Esau is βέβηλος (bebēlos).
It carries the sense of being profane or irreverent toward sacred things.
The writer's concern is not merely that Esau made an unwise bargain.
It is that he treated a sacred privilege as though it were ordinary and expendable.
Hebrews then recalls how Esau later sought the blessing with tears.
The passage is serious and has been interpreted in different ways, particularly concerning the statement that he found no place for repentance.
In its Genesis context, Esau could not reverse Isaac's blessing of Jacob, despite his anguish. Hebrews uses that event as a solemn warning against despising spiritual privilege.
We should not twist it into the claim that every person who has sinned deeply is forever beyond God's mercy.
That would contradict the Gospel's invitation to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
But we should also refuse to weaken the warning.
Tears over consequences are not automatically the same as repentance toward God.
Regret can say, "I hate what this cost me."
Repentance says, "I have sinned, and I need God's mercy."
Regret may be concerned primarily with what was lost.
Repentance turns toward the Lord.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story becomes intensely personal.
What have you been treating as ordinary that God calls precious?
Your marriage?
Your integrity?
Your purity?
Your calling?
Your responsibility to your children?
Your commitment to truth?
Your time in Scripture?
Your relationship with Jesus Christ?
What have you been willing to exchange for a moment of satisfaction?
And what have you been calling harmless simply because the consequences have not arrived yet?
There is no need to pretend.
God already knows.
He knows the compromise you have been rationalizing.
He knows the prayer you have been avoiding.
He knows the conviction you keep silencing.
He knows the relationship you are afraid to surrender.
He knows the bitterness you have been carrying.
He knows the difference between the person you present publicly and the battles you fight privately.
And yet the Gospel does not begin with the announcement that sinners must somehow repair themselves before approaching God.
It begins with what God has done through His Son.
Jesus Christ entered a world filled with broken families, sinful desires, betrayal, and human grief.
He did not come merely to give people better advice.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is the difference between mere moral instruction and the Gospel.
The law exposes our sin.
The Gospel announces the Savior who bore sin.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died on the cross for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
We do not receive salvation because our family history is impressive.
We do not receive it because our parents were faithful believers.
We do not receive it because we have never made an Esau-like decision.
We receive salvation by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to a transformed life.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and walk in obedience.
It does not merely comfort us in our compromises.
It calls us out of them.
There is a beautiful contrast here.
Esau's story warns us about a man who treated his birthright lightly.
But the New Testament points believers toward an inheritance that comes through Jesus Christ.
First Peter 1:3–4 speaks of a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ and an inheritance that is incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.
Think about that.
Esau's birthright could be sold.
Earthly blessings could become sources of conflict.
Family relationships could fracture.
But the inheritance secured for God's people through the risen Christ rests upon the faithfulness of God.
This is not permission to become careless.
It is a reason to treasure Christ above every temporary appetite.
And if you have already made terrible choices, hear this carefully.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot force people to forget what happened.
You cannot demand that trust return immediately.
You may have to face painful consequences, make restitution, seek forgiveness, and rebuild what your actions damaged.
But your past does not have to become an excuse to reject the Savior today.
The cross does not make sin insignificant. It reveals how serious sin is—and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that human beings can somehow rescue themselves through stronger determination.
Our message is Jesus Christ.
His truth.
His holiness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His mercy toward repentant sinners.
His power to transform lives.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin deserves applause.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
But because the grace of God in Jesus Christ is greater than any story we could have written for ourselves.
Perhaps you are the son or daughter who walked away.
Perhaps you are the parent still praying.
Perhaps you are the husband who regrets what he allowed into his marriage.
Perhaps you are the wife who feels spiritually alone.
Perhaps you have been following Jesus for years, yet something has slowly begun competing with your love for Him.
Or perhaps you are reading this without knowing whether you truly believe at all.
Whatever brought you here, do not miss the central question.
Not merely, "How old was Esau when he married?"
But, "What am I doing with the spiritual privileges and opportunities God has placed before me?"
Because knowing the answer to a Bible question is not the same as allowing God's Word to examine your heart.
And information alone cannot save your soul.
Jesus Christ can.
If you recognize sin in your life, confess it to God.
Do not hide behind religious appearances.
Do not use someone else's failures to excuse your own.
Turn to Christ in repentance and faith.
If you have wounded people, take responsibility where you can.
If you have been wounded, seek the Lord's wisdom for forgiveness, healing, and healthy boundaries.
If you are praying for a loved one who has wandered, keep bringing that person before God without confusing love with control.
And if your heart has become cold toward Scripture, begin again.
Open the Bible.
Read it carefully.
Pray for understanding.
Listen to what God has actually said, rather than only what you wish He had said.
There is something deeply humbling about realizing that a verse written thousands of years ago can expose a struggle we thought nobody understood.
Forty years old.
Two wives.
One grieving household.
And a warning that still reaches us today.
But I don't want this story to end with Esau's age.
I want it to lead us to the One who is greater than every patriarch, greater than every earthly inheritance, and greater than every failure we have ever committed.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The Shepherd who seeks the lost.
The Lord who deserves more than the leftovers of our attention.
The King who is worthy of our lives.
And because this truth matters, I want to ask something of you.
Not as a demand.
Not as a way to earn God's favor.
But as an invitation to help carry the message of Christ to people who may never walk into a church, open a Bible, or admit publicly that their hearts are breaking.
One simple share can place Scripture in front of someone who desperately needs it.
You may never know who reads it in silence.
A struggling father.
A grieving mother.
A young person drifting from faith.
A believer wrestling with temptation.
Someone who has been hiding their guilt behind a smile.
And I want to invite you to do something even more personal.
Have you ever watched someone you love make decisions that broke your heart? Or have you been the one who ignored wise counsel and later regretted it?
If you are comfortable sharing, tell us what God has been teaching you.
You do not need to reveal private details or confess sensitive matters publicly. God hears the prayer you cannot put into a comment.
But your testimony, your encouragement, or even a sincere request for prayer may remind another person that they are not alone in their struggle.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is not reduced to inspirational slogans, where difficult passages are not avoided, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center.
There is also a deeper way you can help sustain this mission.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to make that support part of their regular giving.
But I want to be biblically careful about something important.
It does not purchase forgiveness, salvation, spiritual favor, or a closer relationship with Jesus.
And it should never replace the responsibility to care for your family, fulfill your obligations, or faithfully support your local church.
The Bible teaches that Christian giving should be willing and sincere, not driven by guilt or pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
These items are simply resources and expressions of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
The message matters infinitely more than the merchandise.
These resources are intended to help believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ, strengthening their understanding of Scripture, and nourishing their daily walk with God.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
And above all, your relationship with Jesus Christ matters.
Our hope must rest in Christ alone.
And the life of genuine faith bears fruit through love, obedience, generosity, repentance, and perseverance.
That is the kind of discipleship we want to encourage.
Now, before you leave, return with me to the beginning.
A man was forty years old.
He married two women.
His parents grieved.
The Bible preserved the account.
And thousands of years later, we are still learning from it.
Why?
Because the human heart has not changed.
We still struggle with appetite.
We still wrestle with family expectations.
We still confuse immediate satisfaction with lasting joy.
We still make decisions without fully considering what they may cost.
And we still need the mercy of God.
But there is something Esau's story cannot give us by itself.
The final answer to human sin.
For that, we must look to Jesus.
The One who did not despise the Father's will.
The One who obeyed where we have failed.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who offers forgiveness and new life to those who repent and believe.
So do not merely remember that Esau was forty.
Remember what his story warns you not to take lightly.
Remember that spiritual privilege is a responsibility, not a decoration.
Remember that decisions have consequences.
Remember that families need truth and grace.
Remember that no earthly relationship should take the place of obedience to God.
And remember that even when your life has become a story of regret, Jesus Christ is still the Savior to whom you are called to turn.
You may not be able to recover every opportunity you wasted.
You may not be able to repair every consequence overnight.
But you can stop running from the truth.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can take the next faithful step.
And you can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Esau was forty when he made the marriages recorded in Genesis 26:34—but whatever your age today, don't wait another forty years to give Jesus the place in your heart that has always belonged to Him.
